summary: This chapter explains the scientific concept of temperature as a reliable measure of hotness or coldness, contrasting it with unreliable human touch sensations. Through dipping hand experiments, students discover that sense of touch can be tricked. It covers clinical, digital, laboratory, and room thermometers, proper procedures for reading liquid levels without parallax errors, weather reporting, and tracking maximum-minimum daily temperatures.
topic_hierarchy: 7.1 Sense of Touch vs. Temperature - Limitations of skin sensation.
7.2 Scientific Temperature - Definition, units (°C), and thermometers.
7.3 Types of Thermometers - Clinical, digital, laboratory, and room thermometers.
7.4 Weather and Maximum-Minimum Temperatures - 10-day weather tracking.

glossary.definition: A reliable quantitative measure of the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
glossary.example: Boiling water at 100°C or normal human body temperature at 37°C.

glossary.definition: A calibrated instrument used to measure temperature.
A long glass thermometer used in labs to measure liquid temperatures across wide ranges.

experiments_and_activities.aim: To demonstrate that sense of touch is unreliable for measuring temperature.
procedure: Dip left hand in cold water A and right hand in hot water C for 2 minutes.
Simultaneously dip both hands into lukewarm water B.
experiments_and_activities.observations: The left hand feels water B is warm, while the right hand feels the exact same water B is cold.
experiments_and_activities.conclusion: Touch is relative; a calibrated thermometer is required for accurate temperature measurement.

diagrams.description: Illustrates touch experiment setup and correct eye placement for reading a laboratory thermometer.

side_boxes.content: Keep the thermometer vertical and ensure your eye level is directly inline with the top of the liquid column to avoid parallax errors.

misconceptions.error: A laboratory thermometer can be removed from hot water to read its temperature.
misconceptions.correction: Unlike clinical thermometers, standard lab thermometers must remain in the liquid while taking the reading, as the mercury column drops immediately upon removal.

reasoning_qa.question: Why do different students record slightly different readings for boiling water temperature in class?
reasoning_qa.answer: Variations occur due to improper line-of-sight angle (parallax error), touching the beaker bottom with the bulb, or reading after removing the stem.
